title: 9 Popular Leadership Rules That Are Dead Wrong
author: The Good Boss
summary: Gaurav Jain takes nine widely repeated leadership rules and argues that, applied literally, each one backfires. The list covers the customer is always right, move fast and break things, leaders eat last, give 100 percent all the time, never play favorites, do not get too close to your team, always be positive, good leaders never doubt themselves, and reward results not effort. For each he names the damage the rule causes and then offers a corrective, such as being fair but not equal, moving fast only with purpose, or rewarding learning as well as outcomes. The move he makes is to keep the spirit of each maxim while removing its extreme form. The common thread is that sustainable, honest and human leadership beats slogans.
points: Taking servant maxims like leaders eat last literally turns leaders into burned-out martyrs who cannot serve anyone.
Treating fairness as equality ignores individual strengths and needs, leaving high performers unrewarded and low performers unchallenged.
Always demanding 100 percent makes recovery look like weakness and burnout a badge of honor.
Self-doubt is normal for leaders, and normalizing it while asking for input is healthier than projecting certainty.
Rewarding only results kills experimentation, so initiative, curiosity and learning from failed experiments deserve recognition too.
quotes: Prioritize your customers, but don’t worship them. Do what’s right for the business, while taking care of your team.
But here’s the trap: some leaders take this so literally, they become martyrs.
But if you’re always hustling, you’re going to burn out yourself and your team, and it’s not sustainable. This behavior signals your team that rest is failure.
Be fair, but not equal. Give more attention to people who need the support. Support each person based on what they need, not what looks ‘even’.
Optimism is a good thing, but when taken to the extreme, it can kill honest, real conversations.
Real confidence isn’t the absence of doubt. It’s the ability to move forward with it.

Only rewarding outcomes sounds bold and efficient, but it kills experimentation. Because smart experiments often fail, and if you’re only chasing successful outcomes, you will miss out on learning from those experiments.
